chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Ja'far ibn Muhammad al-Ash'ari, from Ibn al-Qaddah, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), that he used to dislike
the qaza' (partly shaven head) in the heads of the children, and mentioned that the qaza' is that the head is shaved except for a little, and the middle of the head is left, it is named the qaza'ah.

key_terms.الْقَزَعَ: Qaza' (a style of shaving the head leaving a patch)

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on leaving a patch of hair unshaven on a child's head?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) discouraged the practice of 'qaza''—shaving most of the head while leaving a small patch or the middle part unshaven—among children, viewing it as a distinctive mark of pre-Islamic ignorance or specific cultural affectation. This ruling highlights the Shia emphasis on modesty and the rejection of vanity in grooming, ensuring that children's appearance remains natural and dignified rather than imitating distinctive tribal or pagan styles.

en.hubeali:
Ali Bin Ibrahim, form his father, from Ja’far Bin Muhammad Al Ashary, from Ibn Al Qaddah, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> that he<sup>asws</sup> used to dislike

the cracked (shaving) in the heads of the children, and mentioned that the cracked (shaving) is that the head is only shaved a little, and the middle of the head is left, it is named as the cracked (shaving)’.
en.sarwar: 2. Ali ibn Ibrahim has narrated from his father from Abu Ja‘far ibn Muhammad al-Ash‘ariy from ibn al-Qaddah who has narrated the following: “Abu ‘ Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, disliked
shaving the head of a child a little and leaving the top middle of the head unshaved, which is called a/-Qaza’.’”
